ABSTRACT
•  Ferroelectric diodes based on silicon foundry-compatible materials such as HZO, AlScN and van der Waals ferroelectrics offer selector-
free, energy-efficient, non-volatile memory solutions for compute-in-memory applications.
•  We present material and interface engineering strategies to improve device performance and reliability.
Recent advances in silicon foundry-process compatible ferroelectric (FE) thin films have reinvigorated interest in FE-based non-volatile memory 
(NVM) devices. Ferroelectric diodes (FeDs) are two-terminal NVM devices exhibiting rectifying current–voltage hysteretic characteristics that 
enable self-selecting designs critical for high-density memory. We examine progress in FeDs based on CMOS-compatible HZO, AlScN, and 
emerging van der Waals ferroelectrics. While FeDs demonstrate promising ON/OFF ratios and rectification capabilities, they face persistent 
challenges including limited write-cycling endurance, elevated operating voltages, and insufficient read currents. We provide materials-focused 
strategies to enhance reliability and performance of FeDs for energy-efficient electronic memory applications, with emphasis on their unique 
self-rectifying capabilities that eliminate the need for selector elements in crossbar arrays for compute-in-memory applications.
Keywords  2D materials · electronic material · ferroelectricity · neuromorphic · heterostructure · nanoelectronics
Discussion
•	 With the shift toward heterogeneous 3D integration in industry roadmaps, there is a pressing need to demonstrate ferrodiode arrays using 
foundry-compatible, back-end-of-line processes to evaluate scalability, yield, and manufacturability.
•	 Sustainability metrics such as energy efficiency, recyclability, and long-term reliability should be adopted as standardized benchmarks in 
assessing next-generation non-volatile memory technologies for neuromorphic computing.

Introduction
The energy consumption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) com-
puting models presents significant sustainability challenges, with 
over 50% of this energy expended in memory access operations 
driven by data movement between computing and memory hard-
ware.1 While CMOS-compatible flash memory serves as the domi-
nant non-volatile memory (NVM) technology, its microsecond-
range access times lag behind main memory’s nanosecond-range 
operation, limiting data retrieval speeds and increasing power 
consumption.2,3 Vertical hetero-integration of logic and memory 
to reduce separation distances to micrometers (μm) could enable 
high-bandwidth data transfer in a near-memory computing archi-
tecture beneficial for data-intensive operations.4,5
Crossbar arrays of two-terminal resistive NVMs represent a 
promising approach for data-intensive near-memory comput-
ing.5 Ferroelectrics (FEs) offer ideal attributes for resistive NVM 
due to their bistable crystal structure ensuring non-volatility, 
non-destructive readout, and long data retention, while their 
ultrafast electric field driven switching (< 1 ns) minimizes write 
energy.6–10 Despite recognition of their suitability for memory 
applications since the 1950s, conventional inorganic perovskite 
FEs such as Barium Titanate ­BaTiO3 (BTO), Strontium Bis-
muth Tantalate ­SrBi2Ta2O9 (SBT) and Lead Zirconium Titan-
ate Pb(Zr,Ti)O3 (PZT) have proven difficult to integrate with 
semiconductor processes due to volatile and highly diffusive ele-
ments. The recent discovery of CMOS-compatible FEs, including 
­HfxZr(1-x)O2 (HZO), AlScN, and van der Waals (vdW) FEs, has 
revitalized interest in FE-based NVM devices.11–13
FE-based NVM devices can be classified into three categories 
based on readout mechanisms: (i) Ferroelectric random-access 
memory (FeRAM), relying on direct readout of switched polari-
zation charge as a current pulse; (ii) Ferroelectric field effect 
transistors (FeFETs), which read polarization coupled with 
channel resistance; and (iii) Ferroelectric resistive memory, 
which reads current flowing through a FE layer. While the first 
two categories appear on major semiconductor technology road-
maps and in industry pipelines,14 resistive memories based on 
CMOS-compatible ultrathin FEs such as ferroelectric tunnel 
junctions (FTJs) and ferroelectric diodes (FeDs) remain emerg-
ing technologies requiring further development.
This perspective focuses on FeDs, highlighting their progress 
and challenges for electronic memory development. FeDs share a 
two-terminal design with FTJs, offering high-density integration 
potential in crossbar arrays, but fundamentally differ in their car-
rier transport mechanisms and circuit function. We examine key 
materials challenges in FeD development and benchmark their 
performance against state-of-the-art resistive memories. We dis-
cuss strategies to enhance performance and reliability, including 
controlled doping to increase ON current, defect reduction to 
improve endurance, and engineering clean metal-FE interfaces 
to enhance ON/OFF and rectification ratios. Notably, we high-
light FeDs’ unique self-rectifying feature, which eliminates the 
need for additional selector elements in crossbar arrays—crucial 
for preventing unwanted sneak path leakage currents—enabling 
higher-density memory architectures.
What is a ferrodiode?
The simplest structure for a FeDs is similar to a FTJ, a Metal-
FE-Metal (MFM) configuration, and its operation is based on the 
concept proposed by Esaki in 1971.15 Device switching relies on 
the ‘electroresistance effect’ where the height of the potential 
barrier between the two metal electrodes depends on the direc-
tion of the FE polarization, modulating the current flowing 
through the barrier.16 Electroresistance is defined as the ratio 
of the current flow in the two opposite FE polarization states. 
A key requirement for the electroresistance effect is asymmetry 
in the potential barrier profile. This asymmetry leads to uneven 
charge screening when FE polarization is switched—resulting in 
barrier height modulation.16 The asymmetry can be designed by 
selecting top and bottom metal electrodes (with different screen-
ing lengths), interface engineering via surface termination or 
the insertion of ultrathin spacer layers.16
The fundamental difference between FTJs and FeDs lies in 
their transport mechanisms, which depend on the thickness of 
the FE layer. As illustrated in Fig. 1a (right), the FE layer in an 
FTJ is ultrathin (< 5 nm), allowing it to be fully carrier depleted. 
Charge transport occurs through direct quantum mechani-
cal tunneling (Fig. 1b, right). The tunnel resistance depends 
exponentially on the square root of the barrier height, creating 
distinct ON and OFF states.17 Fig. 1c (right) describes the cur-
rent–voltage (I–V) characteristics of an FTJ. Initially, an applied 
negative voltage aligns the net polarization upward (FE is in OFF 
state). As a positive voltage is applied above the coercive field, 
the net polarization switches downwards (FE is in ON state), 
leading to high tunnel current. The high ON current persists 
until a negative voltage that causes polarization reversal is 
applied (FE is in OFF state), reducing the current flow.
In the case of FeDs, the FE layer is thicker (> 5 nm), exceeding 
the ‘direct tunneling’ limit. As a result, the charge transport is 
governed by polarization dependent leakage mechanisms such 
as defect-assisted tunneling and Poole–Frenkel (PF) ­emission18 
(Fig. 1b, left). Since the FE thickness in a FeD exceeds the deple-
tion width, carrier transport is highly sensitive to the interface 
Schottky barrier, leading to a strong non-linearity and asymmet-
ric diode like rectifying I–V characteristics. A choice of a suit-
able insulating interlayer that does not substantially affect the 
FE polarization can offer additional pathways to control the non-
linear carrier transport (Fig. 1a, left). Figure 1c (left) illustrates 
the I–V characteristics for a FeD. Initially, applying a negative 
voltage aligns the net polarization upward (FE is in OFF state). 
As the applied voltage increases in the forward direction, the 
device initially conducts low current. Once the electric field sur-
passes the coercive threshold, the internal ferroelectric dipoles 
reorient, flipping the net polarization downward. This transition 
alters the diode’s behavior, switching it from a low-conducting 
(OFF) to a high-conducting (ON) forward state. This polariza-
tion reversal underpins the fundamental ON/OFF switching 
mechanism of the FeD. When the voltage is swept in the opposite 
(negative) direction, the polarization and diode characteristics 
also reverse, leading to a transition from an ON to an OFF state 
in the reverse bias. The non-linear I–V characteristics offer an

advantage for implementing FeDs in a crossbar architecture. In 
conventional crossbar arrays, memory cells are arranged at the 
intersections of perpendicular word and bit lines, and without 
selectors, unwanted ‘sneak path’ currents can flow through unse-
lected cells during read/write operations, that disrupts precise 
resistance modulation of the array and errors while reading the 
resistance state of the selected cell.19 The sneak path currents 
also lead to high energy consumption. Selector devices are typi-
cally used to suppress these parasitic currents, but they increase 
circuit complexity and footprint. The self-rectifying I–V charac-
teristics of FeDs precludes the need for an additional selector 
element (often a transistor), reducing cell structure complexity 
from 1T1R to 1R (Fig. 2). Selector-less crossbar architectures 
with self-rectifying/non-linear FeD devices suppress sneak 
path leakage by leveraging inherent device physics. The non-
linear I–V characteristics (e.g., exponential threshold switching) 
ensure minimal off-state current when unselected cells experi-
ence sub-threshold voltages during read/write operations. 
Self-rectification introduces directional conductivity asymme-
try, preventing reverse-bias leakage pathways while enabling 
forward-bias access to target cells—effectively isolating adjacent 
lines without requiring dedicated selector transistors. FeD cross-
bars theoretically enable ≥ 10X higher areal density than other 
NVM arrays by eliminating separate selector transistors and lev-
eraging ­4F2 cell sizes through vertical stacking of self-rectifying 
ferroelectric junctions.20,21

Materials for FeDs
In this section, we discuss the progress achieved with the 
fabrication and characterization of CMOS-compatible materials 
for FeDs. FeDs were first demonstrated in inorganic perovskite 
oxides such as ­BiFeO3 (BFO) and PZT in the 1990s.22 However, 
challenges with CMOS-integration limited efforts to optimize 
FeD memory performance, despite their self-rectifying char-
acteristics. Over the past five years, FeDs have gained renewed 
interest, driven by the rise of CMOS-compatible FEs. The field 
remains in its early stages and requires materials optimization 
for improved memory performance and reliability.
Figure 3 highlights FeDs based on CMOS-compatible FEs, 
including HZO, AlScN, and vdW FE ­CuInP2S6 (CIPS). The FE 
properties of these materials, and the progress in growth and 
characterization have been discussed in previous review arti-
cles.11–13 Briefly, FE in HZO arises from the stabilization of the 
non-centrosymmetric orthorhombic phase (Fig. 3a). HZO thin 
films (thicknesses between 5 and 15 nm) are commonly synthe-
sized using atomic layer deposition at temperatures < 300 °C, fol-
lowed by rapid thermal annealing at 400–500 °C to stabilize the 
polar orthorhombic phase.20,23 These films exhibit switchable 
polarization of ~ 20 μC/cm2, extracted using polarization versus 
electric field measurements. A 10 nm thick HZO FeD with TiN 
top and bottom electrodes has demonstrated an ON/OFF ratio 
of ~ ­104 and a rectification ratio of ~ 100 (Fig. 3d).20
The remarkable FE properties of wurtzite-structured AlScN 
(Fig. 3b) were discovered in 2019.26 AlScN exhibits a remanent 
polarization of ~ 50–100 μC/cm2 and a coercive field of 2–4.5 
MV/cm, making it suitable for electronic memory applications. 
20 nm thick AlScN films with remanent polarization ­(Pr) ~ 100 
mC/cm2 are routinely grown using magnetron sputtering at 
350 °C.24 However, AlScN films down to 5 nm films have also 
been grown using same conditions which exhibit a ­Pr ~ 100 mC/
cm2 when measured with positive up negative down (PUND) 
pulsing scheme.27 AlScN-based FeDs have achieved ON/OFF 
ratios of ~ ­105 and rectification ratios of ~ ­103 (Fig. 3e) 24 The use 
of a native oxide interlayer (IL) such as ­AlOx or ­HfOx deposited 
using ALD between the AlScN layer and the top Pt metal contact 
introduces asymmetry in the Schottky barrier height, improv-
ing ON/OFF and rectification ratios beyond those of HZO-based 
FeDs.28 Further, precise control over the IL thickness allows tun-
ing of the interface depletion width and depolarizing field, ena-
bling further modulation of electroresistance, switching voltages 
and FeD non-linearity.28 AlScN ferroelectricity being extremely 
robust to temperatures, has also allowed the use of FeDs for high-
temperature non-volatile memory, currently presenting itself as 
the most reliable and viable information storage mechanism in 
extreme temperature environments.29,30
Emerging vdW FEs such as CIPS, a-In2Se3, have shown robust 
out-of-plane ferroelectricity at room temperature.31 Current 
device demonstrations are reliant on thin films mechanically 
exfoliated from a high-quality bulk crystal. CIPS is a vdW fer-
rielectric (Fig. 3c), where net polarization arises from the out-
of-plane displacement of Cu and In ions in opposite directions 
within sulfur octahedra.32 Compared to AlScN and HZO, CIPS 
exhibits a lower net polarization (~ 4 μC/cm2), reducing sen-
sitivity to depolarization.11 Ferroelectric behavior has been 
confirmed in films as thin as ~ 4 nm using piezo response force 
microscopy (PFM).32 Its layered structure and absence of dan-
gling bonds enable FeDs based on vdW heterostructures. A 
graphene/CIPS/InCo FeD has demonstrated an ON/OFF ratio 
of ~ ­106 and a rectification ratio of ~ 2500 (Fig. 3f).25 The high 
electroresistance and non-linearity arises from (i) ultraclean 
vdW contacts, which eliminate Fermi-level pinning allowing 
effective modulation of the interface Schottky barrier height 
upon FE polarization switching, (ii) semi-metallic graphene 
bottom electrode, exhibiting low quantum capacitance near 
the Dirac point, and (iii) anisotropic electronic properties of 
vdW FEs, where the out-of-plane effective mass is three times 
higher than in the in-plane direction in CIPS, enhancing car-
rier transport in the vertical direction.33 The current–voltage

Current status of FeDs
In this section, we compare the current performance of FeDs 
based on CMOS-compatible FE materials with contemporary 
non-volatile memory technologies. While FeDs have demon-
strated impressive ON/OFF ratios, read/write voltages, further 
optimization is essential to address challenges related to scal-
ability, read currents, data retention, and endurance. Figure 4 
benchmarks the performance of FeDs utilizing CMOS-compat-
ible FEs reported in literature, including perovskite FE oxides 
(BFO, PZT).34–36 In addition, we compare the performance of 
alternative, technologically mature NVM, such as commercially 
fabricated RRAM from SkyWater and TSMC 37–39
FeDs exhibit high ON/OFF ratios exceeding ­105 due to the 
electroresistance effect and low leakage currents in > 5 nm 
thick FE layers. In contrast, metal oxide-based commercial 
RRAM typically achieves ON/OFF ratios around 100 (Fig. 4a). 
Moreover, FeDs exhibit current rectification ratios exceed-
ing 5000, a unique device characteristic absent in most NVM 
devices.20,24,32,34–36,40–44 Compared to FeDs with metallic con-
tacts (MFM structures), those incorporating asymmetric metal 
contacts, insulating interlayers (MFIM structures), or semi-
metallic contacts (MFS structures) exhibit enhanced ON/OFF 
and rectification ratios. As discussed earlier, these high rectifica-
tion ratios inherent to FeDs provide a self-selecting capability, a 
key advantage over alternative NVM technologies, which require 
additional selector circuits to mitigate sneak path current

and reduced write/read voltages. vdW ferroelectrics (e.g., CIPS, 
­In2Se3) have low bandgaps (< 3 eV) and lower operating voltages. 
In contrast, high-bandgap, high coercive field materials such as 
HZO (Eg > 5 eV) and AlScN (Eg > 4 eV) exhibit higher read/write 
voltages for full polarization switching.
A persistent challenge for FeDs has been their low ON cur-
rent, which limits miniaturization. Early demonstrations using 
perovskite oxide FEs exhibited ultralow read current densi-
ties (< 1 A/cm2). As shown in Fig. 4c, most reported FeDs still 
operate below 10 A/cm2—insufficient for detection by periph-
eral circuits in memory chips.20 In comparison, metal oxide-
based commercial RRAMs exhibit higher ON currents around 
­104 A/cm2. The low ON current in FeDs is related to the fun-
damental carrier transport mechanism, which relies on PF 
emission, and defect-assisted tunneling. The large bandgap of 
FE materials results in low carrier density, reducing leakage 
current—a desirable feature for FeFETs and FeRAMs but a draw-
back for FeDs. The highest reported current density (~ 200 A/
cm2) has been observed in HZO-based FeDs, potentially due to 
mobile oxygen vacancies enhancing conduction.20 Addressing 
this limitation will be crucial for FeD miniaturization and inte-
gration with advanced CMOS nodes (< 50 nm). It is expected that 
scaling FeDs to ~ 5 nm Fe thickness could lead to larger read cur-
rents enhancing their read speeds.
Endurance and retention are critical metrics defining the reli-
ability of FeDs for non-volatile memory applications. The longest 
reported endurance without degradation has been demonstrated 
in HZO-based FeDs (~ ­109 cycles),20,23 (Fig. 4d), surpassing com-
mercial foundry-processed RRAM (~ ­106 cycles).45 For endur-
ance, FeDs outperform conventional flash by orders of magni-
tude (> ­109 cycles vs. ~ ­105), attributed to their non-destructive 
polarization reversal mechanisms that avoid hot-carrier injec-
tion or oxide degradation. FeDs based on HZO and AlScN exhibit

The future of FeDs
FeDs have made substantial progress over the past five years 
compared to early demonstrations in the 2000s. Moving for-
ward, the community should focus on addressing the following 
challenges:
Device scalability
Wafer scale growth of HZO and AlScN thin films with robust 
ferroelectric response on CMOS-compatible substrates has been 
demonstrated.13 Future research should leverage this progress 
to fabricate FeD crossbar arrays, evaluate memory capacity, 
and assess device yield and variability. Reproducing current 
FeD performance in miniaturized devices (< 100 nm cell size) 
is essential. For seamless heterogeneous integration, all fabri-
cation steps must adhere to back-end-of-line (BEOL) compat-
ibility, requiring processing temperatures below 400 °C and 
avoiding diffusive or contaminant elements (such as Pb, Bi). For 
HZO-based FeDs synthesized via atomic layer deposition (ALD), 
deposition occurs below 250–300 °C. However, the subsequent 
rapid thermal annealing (RTA) step, essential for stabilizing the 
ferroelectric orthorhombic phase, often exceeds 400–500 °C, 
posing integration challenges. Modified low-temperature pro-
cessing protocols, as recently demonstrated below 300 °C, are 
necessary.47 In contrast, AlScN-based FeDs are fabricated using 
CMOS and BEOL-compatible magnetron sputtering at 350 °C. 
van der Waals (vdW) ferroelectrics are also CMOS compatible 
due to their atomically sharp interfaces and low-temperature 
transferability, but scalable large area growth remains a critical 
challenge for technological adoption.
Response time
Response time is less of a concern for FeDs as FE switching 
is inherently ultrafast (< 1 ns), compared to charge migration-
based NVM devices (> 10 ns response time). HZO-based FeDs 
have already demonstrated ~ 10 ns response time,13,20 and 
AlScN has been shown to switch at 60 ns.27 The switching times 
of FeDs based on vdW FEs need to be estimated as most stud-
ies still rely on dc or ms pulsed measurements. Further, the 
ON/OFF and rectification ratios of FeDs should be assessed 
as a function of switching time with ultrafast (ns) pulsed meas-
urements. The key challenge to fast operation, necessary for 
compute-in-memory applications, is incomplete polarization 
reversal due to imprint effects. Recent advances in interfacial 
engineering (e.g., metal-ferroelectric-semiconductor stacks) 
have improved cycle-to-cycle uniformity by suppressing 
imprint effects, but material-level defects still limit ultimate 
scalability. Addressing these challenges through defect-pas-
sivation techniques or strain-enhanced ferroelectricity could 
further solidify FeDs as a sustainable solution for data-inten-
sive workloads like AI/ML accelerators and edge computing 
devices demanding both longevity and energy efficiency. It 
should however be noted that FeDs have a unique advantage 
in terms of fast operation in read-only operation. Given their 
high ON/OFF ratios and lack of selector devices due to large 
non-linearity and rectifying nature, access times for reading 
FeDs can easily go below 1 ns range.23,48

Metal‑ferroelectric interface
A defect-free metal-ferroelectric interface is crucial for opti-
mizing ON/OFF and rectification ratios, as well as FeD endur-
ance and retention. Interface defects lead to Fermi-level pinning, 
limiting depletion width modulation and polarization switching-
induced barrier height modulation. CIPS FeDs with ultraclean 
vdW metallic contacts have demonstrated superior ON/OFF 
and rectification ratios due to efficient barrier height modula-
tion.25 Additionally, interface defects can trigger the formation 
of conducting filamentary bridges, compromising endurance 
and retention.49 Use of 1–2 nm thick insulator interlayers (IL) 
between the FE and metal contact has shown improvement in 
rectification ratios, as demonstrated in AlScN FeDs.28
Carrier doping
Low carrier density in conventional ferroelectrics results in 
low read currents, posing a challenge for scalability and inte-
gration. Since FeDs rely on leakage currents—often driven by 
defect-assisted tunneling and Poole–Frenkel emission—con-
trolled doping with vacancy defects could enhance conductivity 
and improve read currents. However, increasing carrier concen-
tration must not compromise cycling endurance or device reli-
ability. Raman and XPS analysis should be used to characterize 
doping levels and assess their impact on ferroelectric polariza-
tion and response times. Emerging low-bandgap semiconducting 
ferroelectrics such as 3R-MoS2 could offer higher conductivity, 
which may further improve FeD read currents.50
Density trade‑offs
A unique feature of FeD memory is the ability to partially pro-
gram the ferroelectric layer to achieve intermediate resistance 
states between fully up and fully down polarization states leading 
to multi-bit memory. While the exact mechanism that leads to 
multi-bit memory in FeDs remains unclear, is it expected to be 
constrained as FeD sizes and thickness scale down due to reduc-
tion in the number and size of polar domains. Use of interfacial 
strain or doping could be used to tailor polar domains in scaled 
FeDs and engineer robust multi-bit memory. Predictive device 
modeling remains a critical yet underdeveloped area for FeDs. 
Current compact models can capture the ON/OFF ratios and I–V 
characteristics, and there is a need for physical transport models 
to explain partial switching for multistate operation, that can 
be compatible with Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools.
Outlook
Recent progress in FeDs with CMOS-compatible FEs positions 
them as promising candidates for next-generation low-power, 
high-density non-volatile memory, offering self-selecting capabil-
ities to simplify circuit design. To enable large scale adoption, key 
challenges must be addressed, including interface engineering 
with clean contacts, large area growth of vdW FEs, and improved 
read currents through doping and material innovations. Scaling 
FeDs below 100 nm diameters while maintaining performance 
(operating voltage, ON/OFF ratio, retention and endurance) is 
essential for integration with advanced CMOS nodes, unlocking 
applications in neuromorphic electronics and compute-in-mem-
ory architectures. FeDs hold significant promise for advancing 
sustainable computing technologies due to their inherent advan-
tages in energy efficiency and operational longevity. Compared 
to traditional non-volatile memories like flash, FeDs exhibit 
ultralow switching energies (< 10 fJ/bit in some prototypes) and 
compatibility with sub-1 V operation, which directly reduces 
dynamic power consumption in memory-intensive applications. 
This aligns with global efforts to curb energy demands in data 
centers and edge devices, where memory subsystems account 
for a growing fraction of total power budgets. From a lifecycle 
perspective, it is essential to ensure that FeD fabrication lever-
ages materials such as doped AlN and ­HfO2, CMOS-compatible 
materials already integrated into modern semiconductor pro-
cesses, which minimizes reliance on rare or toxic elements. This 
reduces supply chain risks and mitigates environmental hazards 
associated with material extraction and disposal. Furthermore, 
their high endurance and retention could extend device lifetimes, 
reducing electronic waste generation over time.

Abstract: • Ferroelectric diodes based on silicon foundry-compatible materials such as HZO, AlScN and van der Waals ferroelectrics offer selector- free, energy-efficient, non-volatile memory solutions for compute-in-memory applications. • We present material and interface engineering strategies to improve device performance and reliability. Recent advances in silicon foundry-process compatible ferroelectric (FE) thin films have reinvigorated interest in FE-based non-volatile memory (NVM) devices. Ferroelectric diodes (FeDs) are two-terminal NVM devices exhibiting rectifying current–voltage hysteretic characteristics that enable self-selecting designs critical for high-density memory. We examine progress in FeDs based on CMOS-compatible HZO, AlScN, and emerging van der Waals ferroelectrics. While FeDs demonstrate promising ON/OFF ratios and rectification capabilities, they face persistent challenges including limited write-cycling endurance, elevated operating voltages, and insufficient read currents. We provide materials-focused strategies to enhance reliability and performance of FeDs for energy-efficient electronic memory applications, with emphasis on their unique self-rectifying capabilities that eliminate the need for selector elements in crossbar arrays for compute-in-memory applications.
